item.description:
It took me four attempts to successfully parachute into a Wardogs match. On the first try, I opened my parachute far too early, and was promptly sniped from the sky by one of the many sharpshooters that populate Wardogs' battlefield. The second time, I pulled the ripcord far too late, pancaking into the ground like a camo-clad Wile-E-Coyote. The third time, I pulled the cord only slightly too late. But it turns out "slightly too late" has the same outcome as "very too late" when it comes to parachute jumping.
In all instances though, my skydiving failure was not the end of my game. Like many large-scale shooters, Wardogs' battlegrounds are roamed by medics looking for downed soldiers to revive. Unlike those other shooters, it allows reckless idiots like myself to incentivise medics to revive them, through offering a juicy cash bribe to anyone willing to take on the job.
This is not an isolated feature, either. Wardogs is as much about the exchange of capital as bullets, where the twin goals of factional supremacy and personal profit exist in a fragile alliance. It's an idea that, all at once, makes Wardogs stand out from the pack, slightly breaks it as a shooter, and produces a fascinating, real-time critique of late capitalism and the gig economy.
Wardogs exists at the centre of three other FPS inspirations, two of which are obvious at a glance – DICE's Battlefield series and Bohemia Interactive's more simulationist ArmA. The sole game mode is essentially King of The Hill on a massive scale, with three teams vying for control of a circular zone at the heart of a much larger map. Holding the zone for a set amount of time earns the relevant team a point. The first team to reach 100 points wins.
So far, so familiar. But it's in the Counter-Strike DNA where things start to get interesting. Each of your virtual mercenary's lives begins with a CS-style buy-phase, where you purchase your weapons and equipment using a personal pool of in-game currency. You begin the game with a bank balance of $10,000, which is just about enough to kit yourself out with a rifle, some ammo and a basic revive kit. Once you've graduated beyond the starting-player discount, however, any half decent loadout is going to cost a minimum of $4-5K.
The good news is that doing virtually anything in Wardogs will earn you cash. Killing an enemy? That's money. Assisting in an enemy kill? Also money. Reviving players? Driving them to the battlefield? Constructing bases? Money, money, money. Even idling in the control zone will provide a steady drip-feed of cash, the rate of which is doubled if you enter the far smaller, roaming circle that represents the Hot Zone.
The result of this is the kind of role-diversification you'd get in an ArmA RP server, but with profit as the motivating force. You'll see players dedicate their entire matches to ferrying players to the battlefield, or constructing elaborate fortifications around their team's Forward Operating Base. When every action has an immediate, tangible reward to it, players get involved at every level. You can even tip fellow players for doing a good job in healing you or driving you around.
This flow of capital through the match also has some interesting knock-on effects. You'll see knocked out players engage in tacit bribe wars as they strive to receive medical attention first, as well as medics racing to be the first to revive those premium-offering players.
Honestly, I could dedicate this whole article to discussing Wardogs' cash mechanic. But it's not the only thing that makes Bulkhead's FPS interesting. Wardogs' hybridisation of Battlefield and ArmA is itself noteworthy in how it manages to meld together the best aspects of both.
This begins with the maps themselves, which are huge expanses of rolling countryside. Yet unlike, say, Hell Let Loose: Vietnam, only a small amount of the map is fully utilised during a match. Most of the action is concentrated within the control zone, with the rest of the map only being used by transportation vehicles.
While this may seem wasteful, the superfluous countryside is nonetheless fundamental to contributing to Wardogs' atmosphere. On a run, I prefer to parachute in a few hundred metres outside the control zone. Partly because it's (usually) safer. But also because these areas have the same counterintuitively pastoral vibe of Bohemia's ArmA games, a depiction of the countryside that would lend itself to a great hiking simulator were it not for the whole 'War' thing going on.
I also love how this feeling shifts as you approach the control zone, the breeze and birdsong punctuated by distant explosions and helicopters whirring overhead. Then, as you press over the threshold, you'll hear the snap of a sniper's bullet whizzing past your ear, at which point its heads down, eyes peeled, game on.
In short, Wardogs provides that slow-burn, authentic ArmA feel to warfare, but without a movement and combat system that feels like you're wading through treacle. Movement is pacey and your aim highly responsive, and while there's quite a lot of shooting at dots in the distance, the fact that the control zone tends to centre around urban areas offers frequent opportunities for CQB as well.
Indeed, if you have your own squad or follow one around (which is highly recommended for any Assault player), you'll often find that one feeds into the other. There's a very natural flow to Wardogs' combat, a lot of tentative forward pushes, holing up as you try to oust a sniper from his nest, and diversions as you try to help a fallen player or chase the Hot Zone as it relocates.
It's worth noting that this freewheeling nature also applies to roles and progression as well. There's no class system in Wardogs. Instead, progression and unlocks are governed by the weapons and items you use. There's nothing stopping you from taking an assault rifle into battle for Assault XP, while earning medic XP from your defibrillation pads, or chipping away at Support XP with a building hammer or vehicle repairing wrench.
There are also just lots of neat little touches. When you're building a fortification, for example, little yellow crosses will appear on the structure, hitting which will massively boost the build speed, turning construction into an ad-hoc game of whack-a-mole. Wardogs is also one of the most rewarding games to play as a spotter, as using binoculars to identify enemy aircraft, distant snipers and so forth nets you a cash reward.
It's a captivating, fresh approach to multiplayer FPS, and it's little wonder that it's garnered so much attention. But currently Wardogs does have one big issue, which is that actively trying to win the game is also the least rewarding way to play.
When you enter the control zone, you do so at a considerable financial deficit, so charging into the fray is a good way to drain your bank account (especially if you are, say, nearing forty and have the reflexes of a particularly sleepy koala). So the wise thing to do is just…hang back for a bit, using that time to spot enemies, assist in building a base, or do anything that de-risks that initial investment.
This in itself is fine, and Wardogs' battlefields are such that sitting back and watching things unfold is enjoyable in itself. But since being killed is the only way you can lose money, any player with half a brain will quickly figure out that the best way to make cash in Wardogs is to avoid combat whenever possible. At the most extreme, you'll see scenarios where your team's FOB is crammed with people playing as snipers or builders or drivers dropping off supplies, while the Hot Zone wanders around almost completely uncontested.
It's a fascinating flaw, to the point where calling it a flaw feels like an oversimplification. It feels almost a social experiment. Through its cash mechanic, Wardogs fragments and individualises the win condition of what would otherwise be a team game, and as such, there's less reason to care about whether your side emerges victorious so long as you personally profit.
While this might cause problems from a pragmatic perspective, thematically, it's kind of ingenious. Because of course a bunch of mercenaries are only going to do whatever actions benefit them most. In isolated instances the relationship may be symbiotic, but everyone pursuing their own goals makes directing them to a single, overarching one difficult to achieve. And for a certain, cynical kind of mindset, it's downright satisfying to play the game by actively not playing the game.
To be clear, Bulkhead does try to give players reasons to push their team to victory. Winning teams receive a substantial end game cash bonus, for example. But a 20k win bonus doesn't seem so tempting when you can comfortably make double that by sitting at the back building your little base.
No doubt, Bulkhead will spend much of its early access development tweaking and toying with Wardogs' various systems. But despite and even perhaps because of these issues, I've already had a ton of fun with Wardogs. In what has been a tough year for competitive shooters, Bulkhead's game is a jolt of electricity that's brought it gasping back to life, and I was more than happy to slip it a few quid for the privilege.
A copy of Wardogs was provided for this review by Team17.

item.title: CD Projekt Red has clarified to Eurogamer that "all versions of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt that exist in the world" are to be updated with the free Remastered edition upgrade today. That update, by the way, rolls out from 11am BST. Read more
item.description:
CD Projekt Red has clarified to Eurogamer that "all versions of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt that exist in the world" are to be updated with the free Remastered edition upgrade today. That update, by the way, rolls out from 11am BST.
Said CDPR in a statement: "As of today, all versions of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt that exist in the world - Complete, Game of the Year, and even the base game - will all become this new standard version that includes Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine by default. When The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered launches, all copies on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC will be upgraded for free."
Confirmation comes alongside a list of detailed patch notes for the Remastered update, which clarify a wide array of alterations to the game as well as document specific changes to PC, PlayStation and Switch 2 platforms (there don't appear to be any Xbox-specific changes of note, besides the game now being an Xbox Play Anywhere title).
As I noted in my Witcher 3 Remastered impressions yesterday, it can be tricky to parse what's changed and what hasn't while you play, which is, I suppose, as it should be - these things should be background concerns. One area I had wanted more information is what's actually changed regarding enemy behaviour. Here the patch notes add that "attack patterns, counterattacks, movement, reactions, flight and the application of effects" have been tweaked for "many non-boss monsters", though, understandably, the list doesn't break down the changes enemy by enemy.
It's helpful, too, to see what's changed regarding horse riding on Roach, who apparently has updated collision detection and a "refined" jumping animation. Geralt also has more "polished" mount and dismount animations, a new jump animation of his own, and a new idle animation - things I'd not have noticed otherwise.
The many Photo mode changes are specified, which include placeable props and characters as well as a first-person viewpoint, so you can take a picture as if seeing the world through Geralt's eyes. The new accessibility options are detailed, graphical changes are listed in full, and small details such as DualSense controller haptic feedback on PC are picked out.
Switch 2 gets a whole raft of Joy-Con-related options relating to motion control, mouse control, and touch control, meanwhile, and PS5 gets performance improvements, though the bulk of documented changes relate to graphical modes on PS5 Pro. It's a bumper list.
The Remastered edition of The Witcher 3 affects the entire game, re-texturing and re-lighting a lot of it to make the game look more in keeping with a 2026 release, as well as addressing various gameplay and quality of life concerns. As I said yesterday, it's an extraordinarily generous release, given that it's offered at no cost. Primarily, it paves the way for next year's equally remarkable new game expansion, Songs of the Past, but there's no reason why you can't squeeze in another playthrough ahead of it.

item.title: Sony is introducing a lottery system for PS5 Pros on its Japanese online store for when demand for new consoles outstrips the limited supply. Read more
item.description:
Sony is introducing a lottery system for PS5 Pros on its Japanese online store for when demand for new consoles outstrips the limited supply.
As seen in a new information page on the official Sony website, a post confirms that Sony has begun accepting applications for PS5 Pro purchases.
To apply, you need a Sony account registered in Japan, and have played for more than 60 hours on that account over the past two years. Both appear to be scalping prevention measures, which is great.
Prospective buyers have from today until the 7th October to apply. Here comes the fun part: if the number of applications is larger than the available supply of PS5 Pros, the lottery will be held. Winners will be picked from applicants and messaged on the 26th October. Only these select few will have the pleasure of spending ¥137,980 (around £662 / $876) on a video game console.
Once selected you must hurry. If you don't drop a fat stack of cash within a week you'll lose your chance, and that PS5 Pro will escape your grasp, being thrown back into the lottery pool for another prospective buyer to claim.
I'm of two minds on this story. With supply shortages ongoing, thanks to the AI datacenter boom causing both extreme price rises for gaming hardware as well as stock shrinkage, it sucks to buy a new video game console now. Supply has been a continuous problem for Sony this generation, to the dismay of global gaming enthusiasts.
My other thought is, 'gosh I love a good lottery system'. Square Enix implemented one for Final Fantasy 14's housing system, a game where fierce battles over a limited supply of land raged endlessly. In that game, people used to camp outside of houses they thought would go up for sale. The lottery system took the stress out of their hands: as it does here with the PS5 Pros.

item.title: Naughty Dog fans, pick up your ears - it's been a busy night for fans of the PlayStation studio. First of all, in a letter celebrating The Last of Us Day 2026, studio head Neil Druckmann confirmed that two new projects within The Last of Us universe are in the "very early stages" of development at Naughty Dog. Read more
item.description:
Naughty Dog fans, pick up your ears - it's been a busy night for fans of the PlayStation studio. First of all, in a letter celebrating The Last of Us Day 2026, studio head Neil Druckmann confirmed that two new projects within The Last of Us universe are in the "very early stages" of development at Naughty Dog.
"Since [The Last of Us Part 2 documentary] Grounded 2, we've talked about the possibility of telling more stories in the world of The Last of Us," Druckmann said in a message. "We have a couple of very exciting new projects in very early stages—so we can't say much about them at this point. I will tell you that both projects will expand the canon of The Last of Us beyond [The Last of Us Part 1] and [The Last of Us Part 2].
"The world of The Last of Us means a great deal to us, and we wouldn't return to it unless we had something meaningful to say. We believe these stories are worth telling." It's worth noting that Druckmann never outlines whether these projects are games or not - this could be anything then; more TV, a film, an animation. We'll update you as we learn more.
Elsewhere, the studio shed some light on what's going on with Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet. The game, which apparently 'shows off a different side of Naughty Dog' was initially shown off back in 2024, and we've heard precious little from the title since then. And it seems that isn't going to change any time soon.
"There's an electricity around the studio right now as all the pieces come together, and we're stoked to finally unveil Intergalactic in all its glory," Druckmann later on in the note. "But… we need to cook for just a little bit longer. So we want to set expectations: we're going to be quiet for the rest of this year. In 2027, that changes. We'll fully reveal Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet and give you a proper look at Jordan's wild sci-fi adventure. We know it's been a long time since we've had much to share with you. We don't take your continued support for granted. We're working incredibly hard to make something worthy of your patience."
At least we got some moody, new art to tide us over (above). It shows protagonist Jordan, with her trademark sword, looking into a large wooded area that has been taken over by some kind of red alien matter. I hope that's enough to tide you over until we see whatever it is that Naughty Dog has been cooking next year.

item.title: Just days after announcing a silly skin off toggle for Call of Duty: Warzone, Activision has returned to share some even better news for Modern Warfare 4. At launch and beyond, double XP tokens will count down only when you're actively in a match, not in real-world time. Read more
item.description:
Just days after announcing a silly skin off toggle for Call of Duty: Warzone, Activision has returned to share some even better news for Modern Warfare 4. At launch and beyond, double XP tokens will count down only when you're actively in a match, not in real-world time.
Call of Duty's official X account delivered the news succinctly, confirming that existing tokens - ones you may have accrued from previous COD titles or Warzone - will also be usable in Modern Warfare 4.
Previously, activating a double XP token would begin the countdown immediately. If you need to get up from your chair, take too long building a loadout or idle as you wait for a friend to join, all that time will be wasted as tokens continue to deplete in the background. It's something that's been universally disliked for obvious reasons, and players have called on Activision to change the way it works with each new yearly COD release.
The issue also isn't exclusive to Call of Duty; rival franchise Battlefield treats double XP tokens the same way, and its community is similarly frustrated. Battlefield Studios recently made players even more upset by sending an in-game message promising to change tokens so they count down in-match, before saying it was an error - twice.
As we approach the launch of Modern Warfare 4, Activision seems to be doing its best to convince lapsed players to return. Since the game's reveal, we've seen a pre-order loyalty discount, the introduction of a skin toggle in Warzone, developer updates about the game's matchmaking algorithm, and now this double XP token change - all things that mainly benefit longtime players who may be disillusioned with the series.
Modern Warfare 4 releases 23rd October on PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch 2.

item.title: Double Fine's wasted no time at all as an independent game studio (again) after splitting from former owner Xbox earlier this summer. The storied developer is releasing its whacky driving sim, Thank You Bus Driver, in roughly two weeks time. Read more
item.description:
Double Fine's wasted no time at all as an independent game studio (again) after splitting from former owner Xbox earlier this summer. The storied developer is releasing its whacky driving sim, Thank You Bus Driver, in roughly two weeks time.
Announced mere weeks ago, Double Fine's first post-Xbox release is a black-and-white "chaotic bus driving game where you take on the role of a town's bus driver just trying to get through the day with minimal rule breaking and maximum gratitude." And, as the studio announced this weekend, it's coming to various PC storefronts on 14 October.
You can find Thank You Bus Driver on Steam, GOG and Itch.io.
Thank You Bus Driver asks you to take passengers to their destinations within a time limit, but the comedy simulation game has an unexpected dash of Paper, Please as well. As the day goes on, you'll need to enforce various rules by turning around and slapping passengers across the face with your freakishly long arms - in case you were wondering where the signature Double Fine twist was hiding.
Of course, this also marks Double Fine's first game since regaining its independence. Xbox's ongoing corporate restructure has seen the console maker spin off five first-party studios, including Double Fine, with plans to lay off around 3,200 staff by next summer. The Psychonauts and Brutal Legend studio laid off a quarter of its own workforce as a result.
So, this time around, Double Fine is delivering Thank You Bus Driver differently. The game is set to launch Double Fine Action Labs, a label for "weird, little games" that can come to fruition much quicker than you'd expect. The developer's new Amnesia Fortnight Kickstarter campaign will likely yield another Action Labs entrant, too.
Tim Schafer - the studio's founder and the beloved designer behind many of its biggest games - recently said there was no ill will between Xbox and Double Fine. "I love it as an idea," he said of subscription service Game Pass. "I liked it for Double Fine games. If you're sitting in a store and holding a disc, and it costs $70, and it's about a walking lighthouse, there's a barrier there. But if you've just got to download a game you've already paid for, it might lead people to trying weird games like Double Fine makes. So I'm very pro Game Pass, and hope it succeeds and goes forward."
Asked about why the games industry seems so fragile nowadays, Schafer was unsure: "People are playing games, people are making money, so I don't know why there is a big loss of jobs. I assume someone is being greedy somewhere."

item.title: "What if London existed in the Grand Theft Auto universe? What if Rockstar created a GTA game set in London?" Anyone sitting in the venn diagram centre of GTA fan and cartography sicko might be happy to learn that YouTuber CityEd has answered both of those questions with a GTA-style map. Read more
item.description:
"What if London existed in the Grand Theft Auto universe? What if Rockstar created a GTA game set in London?" Anyone sitting in the venn diagram centre of GTA fan and cartography sicko might be happy to learn that YouTuber CityEd has answered both of those questions with a GTA-style map.
"I've created a GTA-ised map of London imagining how the map would look, and re-invented place names in a classic GTA style," CityEd wrote on their Patreon, where you can also find a PDF copy of their map. "For instance, Kings Cross becomes 'Dukes Cross', Angel becomes 'Saint'', and the whole city becomes 'Trafalgar'."
CityEd's thought experiment aimed to carry Rockstar Games' naming conventions across the pond - that includes the developer's signature satire, "exaggerated landmarks and GTA-style cartography" - using the studio's past games as a reference point.
"While the cities and places they base their maps on exist in real life, they have this fun convention for creating fictional place names where they find something historically or culturally associated with the place, exaggerate it, and use that instead," they explained.
As they also noted, Rockstar's last trip to the English capital wasn't much help at all. 1999's GTA: London mission pack didn't bother renaming the city in fun ways, so CityEd's version had to start from scratch.
Good thing, too, because their map is a really cool look at what could've been. A longer 30-min video delves into CityEd's process, and explains how they used the real-world history of certain locations to inform their own map.
We won't need to wait much longer for our next actual Grand Theft Auto map, either. GTA 6 is coming out in under two months with a map big enough to fit at least two GTA 5s in it. Eager internet sleuths haven't been able to work out if a famous Florida locale made the cut, though.

item.title: Ubisoft is internally calling its latest generative-AI initiative 'Motherbrain' - you know, like the evil supercomputer turned gross brain-in-a-jar monster from Nintendo's Metroid series - according to trademarks filed by the Assassin's Creed and Far Cry publisher. Read more
item.description:
Ubisoft is internally calling its latest generative-AI initiative 'Motherbrain' - you know, like the evil supercomputer turned gross brain-in-a-jar monster from Nintendo's Metroid series - according to trademarks filed by the Assassin's Creed and Far Cry publisher.
As first reported on by The Game File and spotted by Kotaku, a bunch of recent trademark applications use the definitely-not-ominous Motherbrain term to refer to the company's various gen-AI plans.
According to the report, one trademark makes mention of a "downloadable computer software using artificial intelligence (AI) for creating video games and interactive content." Another refers to an AI service used for both "analyzing data and interacting with humans," and the research and design of "software using artificial intelligence."
Ubisoft hasn't mentioned Motherbrain to the public just yet. The term is seemingly only being used inside of the publisher's walls, but Ubisoft's been pretty openly enthusiastic about the controversial tech and its possible applications in game development for a while.
Back in 2023, Ubisoft unveiled a gen-AI ghostwriting tool - elegantly named Ghostwriter - that would supposedly help game developers come up with background dialogue for in-game NPCs. Late last year, Ubisoft CEO Yves Guillemot claimed generative AI had rolled out across the entire company and called it a "revolution" on the same scale as the jump from 2D to 3D games. And, just this summer, the publisher said it was "accelerating" investment into Teammates, a shooter billed as Ubisoft's "first playable generative AI experience."
Will the initiative eventually transform into a spiky-haired, one-eyed brain? Only time will tell.
This all comes after Ubisoft closed two studios, canned six projects and laid off developers as part of its so-called major restructuring in January of this year. A few months back, the publisher shut down another pair of studios and restructured a third in a move that also cut around 380 jobs.

item.title: It's tricky to appraise the Remastered edition of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt because on the one hand, everything about it is extraordinary. It's a free upgrade to an 11-year-old game that showcases a level of support and generosity I don't think I've seen for any other single-player game, ever. item.description:
It's tricky to appraise the Remastered edition of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt because on the one hand, everything about it is extraordinary. It's a free upgrade to an 11-year-old game that showcases a level of support and generosity I don't think I've seen for any other single-player game, ever. It's remarkable that The Witcher 3 should be visually overhauled and even systemically altered so long after its release, without a cost to the player attached.
However, it does also feel a bit purposeless without a Songs of the Past expansion to play with it - assuming you weren't already considering a replay of the game, or going back to finish the main campaign (which you need to have finished for Songs of the Past), or playing the expansions. All good reasons to go back. What I'm saying is that alone, if you've already played it before, the Remastered edition won't necessarily keep you entertained for longer than a few hours while you tour the game to see what's new.
To put it more bluntly, the Remastered edition doesn't fundamentally change The Witcher 3. If you were somehow hoping this remaster overhauls the game's combat, for example, I'm sorry to tell you that it doesn't. Indeed, it can be quite challenging to work out what is actually new when you're playing it. Most of the time, it's The Witcher 3 game we all remember, however long the list of changes is - though perhaps it's more accurate to say it's The Witcher 3 that lives in our memory.
You see, before playing the Remastered edition, I loaded the current version of The Witcher 3 to refresh my memory, and even though CD Projekt Red has gone to lengths to update the game over the years, and add new things like ray tracing to it, there's no shaking the feeling it now looks old. Under the cold scrutiny of 2026, the textures are aging, the world is pretty but a bit cardboard-cut-outy, especially the foliage, and the lighting a bit simplistic. No amount of graphical flourishes can change this - it's what's underneath the flourishes that needs to change. And this is what the Remastered edition has done.
Load it and, immediately, there's more detail up close. There's more detail on Geralt's scarred body as he bathes in the wooden tub at the beginning of the game, and on the clothes he wears. There's more detail on the mountain as he walks to the balcony to take a look. There's more detail on his mentor Vesemir's face when he talks to him. All of a sudden, The Witcher 3 bears close scrutiny again. And it's the same all over: environments are sharper and more detailed; wilderness areas are fuller, bushier, and more vibrant. The faces of people you speak to are all improved: no one looks like they were made 10 years ago, in other words. They all look as though they belong in a game now.
Enemies have had visual glow-ups as well. Drowners look more like creatures from the lagoon now, with light-reflecting, iridescent skin. Forktail dragons boast shades of metallic green skin and membranous wings, which flap, chicken-like from their backs. Barghest hellhound dogs have flaming green eyes and leave shadowy trails as they jump. A vampire enemy - who looked exactly like that lady from the A Night to Remember Witcher cinematic - and who kicked my arse a few times, had greying, rotting skin, and disappeared in and out of shimmering thin air. All over the world, there's thrill in simply encountering an old enemy to see what's changed.
Newer lighting techniques frame the world even more picturesquely, even more of the time. The Witcher 3 always excelled visually at dawn and dusk, throwing the game in peachy golden hues, or cutting it through with pale shafts of light, but now those spectacular lightshows reflect on watery surfaces, and forests have more depth because of the shadows cast from them. Similarly, packs of torch-bearing citizens light cities in different ways, while sconces blare moodily in archways, or the moon highlights mist hovering on the harbour. And of course ray tracing and path tracing take this further (should your computer be capable of them, if playing on PC), helping boggy swamps and water-filled areas of the game look more real.
Sidenote: this does come at the cost of performance. My middling computer spluttered hard when I had ray tracing mode turned on in Novigrad, whereas it otherwise handled it okay in the wider world (I haven't had a chance to test it on a base PS5 console yet; apparently PS5 Pro now runs ray tracing at 60 FPS). Still, the graphical changes are such that even with ray tracing turned off, there's a noticeable visual upgrade to the game.
That's nice, but I've always been slightly more interested in what the Remastered edition brings to the game in addition to visual improvements, especially where combat is concerned, and one of the most exciting changes here is reworked skill trees. Whereas you used to have four blocks of abilities - one related to weapons, one to potions, one to magic - you now have those categories but organised into trees, with branching routes you can plot your way around. There still seem to be the same amount of skills though, despite the new layout making it appear as though there are more, and many of the same skills return.
Some skills have changed, though. The crossbow in particular seems to have been improved - it being a little useless before, other than for knocking flying opponents out of the air - and it benefits from some very generous damage multipliers now, especially to headshots. There's a wonderful new ability that gives you a percentage change to kill a ranged attacker if you parry their shot perfectly. There also seems to be a trend towards encouraging build overlap, so having magical or potion-related abilities increase sword damage and vice versa. More theoretical complexity, perhaps, though not a great deal of tangible change after my limited time with it. (I still find the game's ability slotting system, whereby you can only have 12 abilities active at any one time, restrictive. Why not, many years after release, simply remove it? Let people be overpowered.)
Enemy behaviour has also been updated in this Remastered edition, though it's sometimes hard to tell exactly how - it's not specifically detailed anywhere. Accompanying press documentation states: "Formerly routine encounters with enemies like wolves and drowners feel much more immersive and reactive thanks to updated enemy behavior." So I sought out some wolves and drowners to test this, but in both cases I couldn't notice much difference. They did seem more aggressive and more predisposed to dodging - more challenging, in other words - and this is true of all the enemies I encountered in the remastered game. Though whether this is because I'm rusty and jumped into a late-game save, I don't know. Perhaps a bit of both.
The other big combat change is animations. Geralt now pirouettes and slices his sword - and casts his spells - with more fluidity and grace than he did before, but also with zip so you're not slowed down by them. There are more combat finisher moves as well, which usually seem to involve sliced-off limbs, and they help bring visual flair and interest to battles, as you encounter them over and over again. Combat feels refreshed and challenging, if not radically different.
Smaller changes are harder to get a handle on. The Witcher Senses system - whereby you hold a trigger for Geralt to go into detective mode - has been reworked, apparently, requiring you to more specifically focus on clues, but I didn't notice much difference. Similarly, the photo mode has been expanded but I couldn't really tell you how - it looks the same to me. Transmogrification is a more notably new addition to the game, whereby you can change the appearance of your weapons and armour so you don't have to look like a higgledy-piggledy patchwork scarecrow - and this is very welcome, but it's unlikely to make or break your overall adventure.
And so much of that is true of many nips and tucks; there are even features like cross-platform mod support, and a mod area built into the main menu, which are quietly very important additions, but obviously don't do much unless you start interacting with the mods themselves. These are a way to help the game live on for another decade, albeit in the community's hands.
Mostly, the Remastered edition is excellent preparation for what lies ahead, which is Songs of the Past. But it's also a wonderful reminder of how impressive The Witcher 3 still is, and why it's endured. This was already apparent in the game as it was. The world still burped and farted and smeared you with mud as you ran around it, taking you on a fantastical but simultaneously earthly adventure, which felt both more grand and more touchably real than many others.
To stand in Novigrad - one of gaming's great cities - and be surrounded by all that noise and activity, and just the sheer scale of it, is to appreciate, to some degree, the ambition of what CD Projekt Red attempted to make. Then add to that two impressive expansions and there's a generosity of adventure here that's - to suddenly jump back into it - bewildering. By remastering this, and by adding things like a new suite of accessibility options, CD Projekt Red and development partner Yigsoft have ensured The Witcher 3 not only reminds people why it's such an important role-playing game, but that it continues to be one for many years to come.

item.description:
The popular - and always appreciated - seamless co-op mod has finally come to Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin, the only game of the trilogy to have spent years without it. Mod creator Yui, who's responsible for the seamless co-op mods for Dark Souls Remastered, Dark Souls 3, Elden Ring and Armored Core has returned to release the mod's alpha version to the public.
Dark Souls 2 does, of course, support co-op by default. But, as with other FromSoftware-developed games, the process is a little convoluted and comes with a number of limitations that prevent players from being able to play with their friends with no interruptions.
Yui's mods solve that, making it possible to play the game alongside friends (up to five others, in this case) from start to finish in a single session. The mod skirts around many of the game's inherent limitations to do so, removing progression blockers and keeping all players' sessions in sync.
The mod can be downloaded from NexusMods or GitHub. It goes without saying that this alpha version is going to have a few issues, as Yui is using it to test the mod and fix bugs - so don't expect the experience to be quite as seamless as you're used to from her other mods.
Some potential problems include enemy de-sync when a player dies, including when facing bosses such as Velstadt, and Sinh. Certain interactions, such as opening/closing doors or picking up items, may not always be in-sync for all players too.
Yui's Patreon post has a full list of known issues, so it's worth having a look at that before you jump in. The good news is that multiple patches have already been released, so we may not be too far off from the mod's final version.

item.description:
Back in August, CD Projekt Red properly revealed new Witcher 3 expansion Songs of the Past during Gamescom's Opening Night Live show. Whilst I got to experience a hands-off demo of the new content (which I loved), no one in the public has yet had chance to get their hands on the title. So, it seems like CD Projekt Red is doing the next best thing and get our, erm, ears on it instead.
Milan records has today releaseed what it is calling The witcher 3: Wild hunt – Songs of the Past (OST Gamescom 2026 EP). The release is a five-track EP featuring music by Magda Urbańska, Marcin Przybyłowicz and Daniel Elms. Available everywhere now, the EP includes music featured in the upcoming third expansion from the role-playing game that we got a small taste of last month. I think the music sets the tone nicely for the decepticly bucolic environment of Letten; treating us to folksy light-heartedness with an underbelly of malice and mystery.
"Creating music for Songs of the Past was incredibly exciting for me, but I also felt a huge sense of responsibility," notes Magda Urbańska in a press release. "I vividly remember the first time I heard the music from The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — it shook me to the core. That music was extraordinary then, and it remains extraordinary to this day.
"I've worked with classical music for most of my life, but folk requires a completely different sensibility — it has its own tone and form, while also offering enormous creative freedom. But our roots, our Slavic heritage, are something more than that — something that runs deep within us, something that grows out of who we are. I hope we've managed to preserve The Witcher DNA in these pieces."
Elsewhere in the press release, the upcoming tracks from the game are described as "blending evocative orchestral writing with traditional folk influences, powerful vocal performances, and regional instrumentation inspired by the world's diverse cultures" - and you can certainly hear that in the five tracks released today.
Songs of the Past's Gamescom reveal told us quite a few things about this massive expansion - dropping over a decade after the original game came out - confirming the new playable location as Letten, confirming a new romance, noting the story has been in the works for years, and telling us that the whole project came together after a series of happy accidents.

item.title: Diablo 4's Season of Hell's Legacy began over two weeks ago following a banner BlizzCon, but its launch has been surprisingly wobbly. item.description:
Diablo 4's Season of Hell's Legacy began over two weeks ago following a banner BlizzCon, but its launch has been surprisingly wobbly. The season initially suffered a multi-hour delay thanks to log-in errors and server issues, but Blizzard has apologised to players using the power of gifts.
As reported by Icy Veins, a number of players logged into Diablo 4 to see they've received a Resplendent Spark, one of the game's rarest crafting materials.
Through the in-game Horadric Post mailing system - ironically added with the new season, players logged in to see a thank you note alongside the gift. "We're sorry for any unexpected issues you may have experienced," the message reads. "Thank you for standing with us. Please accept this token of appreciation for our journey ahead."
Unfortunately, it doesn't appear that everyone received the gift, even if they may have received the apology message. Players on Reddit theorise only those who were affected by the season's launch issues - such as not being able to claim a Resplendent Spark from the seasonal progression track, actually received the gift. That said, the note is clear about a gift being enclosed, so those left out may have simply run into a server issue.
Resplendent Sparks are one of the most coveted items in Diablo 4. Players typically spend hours grinding challenging endgame content to get a single one. They're used in crafting Mythic Unique weapons and gear - the most powerful in the game.
Although things have stabilised in the days since, launch issues also extended to gameplay mechanics, such as The Tree of Whispers failing to display rewards. As it stands, all outstanding problems have been addressed in patches and hotfixes released in the days following the season's launch.

item.title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is introducing a highly-requested feature to Warzone later this year. With the launch of the game's first season, players will be able to turn off character skins from other Call of Duty games in the free-to-play mode. Read more
item.description:
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is introducing a highly-requested feature to Warzone later this year. With the launch of the game's first season, players will be able to turn off character skins from other Call of Duty games in the free-to-play mode.
When the filter is turned on, you'll only see Modern Warfare 4 character skins in the lobby and matches. This is notable for a number of reasons, not least because developer Infinity Ward committed to taking an "authentic" and "grounded" approach to Modern Warfare 4 skins and future collaborations. In other words, all the skins you're going to see will be the ones that exist in Modern Warfare 4.
"This all-new filter has been built specifically for the Modern Warfare 4 chapter, giving players more control over the operator skins they see in Call of Duty: Warzone only," a post on the official blog reads.
Since its introduction in 2020, Warzone has become a melting pot for yearly Call of Duty releases. The free-to-play mode has accumulated hundreds of character and weapon skins, weapon builds, blueprints and countless cosmetics from various COD titles over the years. Given the differing themes of each game, and each developer's approach to how silly the skins could get, Warzone ended up with an amalgamation of looks that rarely go well together.
As the size of Warzone's skin wardrobe grew, so too did players' desire for a toggle that prevented them from seeing skins they felt didn't fit with the mode's aesthetic. Black Ops 6 and 7, for instance, featured collaborations with American Dad, The Boys, Beavis and Butt-Head and many other franchises whose character and look don't fit with Call of Duty's.
The arrival of the skin toggle is something many thought would never happen, not due to any potential technical hurdles, but simply because a major selling point of those skins is that other players can see you as that character. The filter only turns the skin off for the player who toggles it on, not everyone in the lobby - and crucially not the player who bought said skin.
It's also worth keeping in mind that there's no way for players to know how many of their teammates and enemies in any given match have the filter on or off, a key point those in favour of the filter's existence have relied on in the past.
While the filter is welcome, it doesn't stop Infinity Ward and Activision adding skins players may consider wacky or out-of-place down the line. Indeed, this is not a 'smart' filter that identifies which skins fit and which do not; it simply turns off skins from other games all together.
As it stands, the filter is exclusive to Warzone, but I imagine players will ask for it in Modern Warfare 4 multiplayer if/when post-launch skins arrive which they deem inappropriate for the game's atmosphere.
Modern Warfare 4 arrives 23rd October on PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch 2.

item.description:
Marvel's Wolverine has received a new update that should hopefully bring an end to the "fart gas" scent trails saga. The latest patch, version 1.001.006, includes an option to turn off scent trails for Whiskey Bottle collectibles, Material Crate audio pings as well as Nightmare Door roots using three separate toggles in the Gameplay menu.
Senses will remain for what developer Insomniac Games described in the patch notes as "story-critical" moments, but that should at least be enough to limit how often they are a nuisance.
The game's ever-visible, bright-lit blue trails are meant to help players navigate to the next mission objective and locate collectibles hidden around levels. However, their implementation has been controversial, as many players saw them as unnecessary given how linear the game's levels typically are.
Even before Marvel's Wolverine came out, players asked for a way to turn them off, and though the studio initially released a hotfix to lessen their effect so they're less visible in the world, the game's latest patch delivers on the developer's promise to explore adding an option to turn them off entirely.
Elsewhere in the patch notes, a number of crashes players reported have been fixed, alongside instances where the player could become stuck. Patch 1.001.006 also addresses the overlapping bathroom sign in the casino level, which sparked accusations of generative AI use online.
If you're looking for some help locating Whiskey Bottles, Material Crates or any other in-game collectible, the Eurogamer Marvel's Wolverine guide has pages to help with that alongside a full walkthrough of the game.

item.title: A reported $400 million budget for Hideo Kojima's Physint has already been walked back over the weekend, with multiple outlets now saying Xbox is paying nowhere near that figure for Hideo Kojima's stealth game. Read more
item.description:
A reported $400 million budget for Hideo Kojima's Physint has already been walked back over the weekend, with multiple outlets now saying Xbox is paying nowhere near that figure for Hideo Kojima's stealth game.
The number originated from Christopher Dring of The Game Business, who said on his podcast on Friday that Xbox was "signing Kojima for a project often referred to as Physint with a budget around $400 million".
Later, however, Dring himself clarified on X/Twitter that Xbox is likely paying "quite a bit less" than the figure Kojima had originally quoted Sony - Dring originally said he'd heard "everything from $300 million to $600 million, although it's $400 million that is the figure that is bandied around" - and Bloomberg's Jason Schreier said his own sources described Microsoft's negotiated figure as "significantly less than this".
Windows Central's Jez Corden went further, saying Xbox is paying only a "fraction" of it, although neither source reported an actual figure.
Physint, Kojima Productions' action-espionage title and spiritual successor to Metal Gear Solid, was originally announced as a PlayStation project. Sony reportedly spent months negotiating with the studio before pulling its funding after the project exceeded budget and missed deadlines.
Metal Gear and Death Stranding creator Hideo Kojima has spoken about a number of topics concerning Sony's sudden decision to back away from publishing his tactical espionage project, Physint. It was a decision made in June, and though Kojima was able to convince Xbox to pick up the Metal Gear successor and continue funding and publishing it.
The deal includes movie and TV licensing rights for Physint, along with improved terms for Kojima's other in-development project, the horror game OD.
Xbox is now once again embracing exclusives, notably confirming recently that Xbox games Gears of War: E-Day and Clockwork Revolution won't be released on PlayStation. However, some games such as Forza Horizon 6 and Fable remain in the works for PS5, so there's hope for Physint.
"I think all of that will be announced at a later time," Kojima said when asked recently. "I'm not sure yet, and I can't really say."

item.description:
Minecraft maker Mojang has announced The Sift, a new Minecraft dimension that will join the Overworld, the Nether, and The End when it launches on Java and Bedrock in 2027. It's the first new dimension added to the game since The End arrived in 2011.
The Sift will appear first in Minecraft Dungeons 2, slated for release on 29th September, before coming to the base game next year.
The Sift was announced during Minecraft Live on 26th September, alongside the wider Dungeons 2 reveal. We didn't get much information about it - Mojang is holding back most of the details for now - but did describe it as a new environment that will bring new biomes, mobs, and ways to play and explore. As yet, there's no firm release date.
"Minecraft Live revealed that the newest Minecraft dimension isn't just finding its home in Dungeons 2, it'll also be coming to Minecraft Java & Bedrock Edition next year," the team teased.
"This will be the first new dimension in over 14 years - joining the Overworld, the Nether and the End as our fourth dimension. During the broadcast, you got a glimpse into this dimension in Minecraft - and even one of the mobs that calls it home. But surely that's not enough! Luckily you can experience it for yourself in Minecraft Dungeons 2 - coming September 29, 2026."
We also learned that Minecraft World will open in London at Chessington World of Adventures Resort in 2027, and have "something for every type of player".
"Are you an explorer? Great, this place is enormous. A builder? Let me show you to the world's first Minecraft World Hotel, where you can enjoy meals in a deep-sea diner, recharge in themed rooms, and mingle with mobs. No word on phantoms, but that's mainly because the beds are so comfortable that sleep deprivation has yet to be an issue!"
There'll also be the world's first Minecraft rollercoaster, which is both in- and outdoors and described as "terrifying and thrilling".
Earlier today we reported that more than 300,000 players try Minecraft for the first time every single day. That's according to Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, who announced on Twitter/X over the weekend that despite 17 years and 425 million copies sold, "Minecraft is still finding new players".

item.title: While Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth was "difficult" to Platinum by "design", sequel Revelation's Platinum trophy will be "easier to get". Read more
item.description:
While Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth was "difficult" to Platinum by "design", sequel Revelation's Platinum trophy will be "easier to get".
That's according to director Naoki Hamaguchi, who recently acknowledged that the reason so few players had unlocked Rebirth's Platinum trophy - about 2.6% - is because the team "wanted to make people go through all this content and perfect it".
Now, talking to Anime News Network, Hamaguchi stopped short of calling the tough Platinum requirements "a mistake in judgement", but did admit he had "regrets" when he saw the fan reaction.
"For Rebirth's platinum trophy - well, for Rebirth in general - there's so much to do. There's so much content. We wanted to make people go through all this content and perfect it. It's kind of by design that that would make it difficult," he said.
"So I don't want to call it a mistake in judgment or anything but we also didn't expect so many people to want the platinum trophy. I think that was what we underestimated here. Battle director Teruki Endo also saw [the fan reaction] and was like, 'Oh, no! I feel bad - I have regrets'."
For Revelation, Hamaguchi admits that combat needs to be "enjoyable".
"I think that's one thing that we've learned from Rebirth: to make the battles themselves enjoyable rather than just challenging," he said.
"In comparison, for Revelation, the platinum trophy will be easier to get. In terms of how difficult it will be, we're expecting twenty percent of players or maybe even more than that to be able to obtain it."
Final Fantasy 7 Revelation is due out on 8th April 2027 on Nintendo Switch 2, PC, PS5, and Xbox Series. Our Dom recently spoke to Hamaguchi about whether the game will crumble under its own open-world ambitions, but came away with their mind at ease.

item.title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has praised Xbox's ongoing "streamlining" under Xbox CEO Asha Sharma just days after another round of layoffs hit the division. Read more
item.description:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has praised Xbox's ongoing "streamlining" under Xbox CEO Asha Sharma just days after another round of layoffs hit the division.
Speaking on the Sources podcast with Alex Heath, Nadella was asked about Xbox's ongoing overhaul and the state of the brand and said he felt "fantastic".
"I feel fantastic about the IP we have right now," Nadella said (as transcribed by IG). "If I look at the studios, the IP portfolio we have, and our ability to then take that and produce great games going forward - I feel fantastic. There's some amount of streamlining the team is doing, and Asha is doing, which is great to see."
He continued: "And then we have to invent the right sustainable business model that allows us to deliver gaming to more and more people. That has always been the goal, which is we want to be a great publisher and a great platform provider for games across both PCs and Xboxes.
"So that is sort of our goal, and I think Asha and the team have said that Xbox is going to get back to growth this next fiscal year, and that's the plan they're executing on, and in that process, do a bang-up job of producing some great games."
In July, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced job cuts affecting 3,200 employees as part of what she called the "most significant" restructuring the company had ever undertaken. 1,600 of those layoffs were effective immediately, while some first-party studios, including Double Fine and Compulsion Games, were permitted to go independent again.

item.title: Video game database MobyGames will let developers claim video game credits and customise their personal portfolios, albeit only via a new premium tier. Read more
item.description:
Video game database MobyGames will let developers claim video game credits and customise their personal portfolios, albeit only via a new premium tier.
As reported by our sister site GamesIndustry.biz, MobyGames Professional launched in beta in June, with a full 1.0 version due this autumn. Alongside enabling developers to claim credits of games they've worked on via a verification process, it also lets users build a personal portfolio page on the site.
Speaking to GamesIndustry.biz at Gamescom, product manager Reece Denzel said signups had been "great" and "thousands of developers" have already claimed their pages.
Talking specifically about the verification process behind claiming a page, which stops short of letting anyone edit their actual credit listings, Denzel said: "There's two parts to that. One is making sure that people are who they say they are, and that's a human-driven verification process that we run in the background. When it comes to making sure that credit history is reflected appropriately, the actual way that we do credits and credit verifications has not changed: It's not changed since Atari has been involved, it's not changed in a long time, and we have no plans to change that process". Atari acquired MobyGames in March 2022.
"It's very important for us to note that that does not give them the ability to edit any of the structural information about things like their credits," Denzel added. "What it does give them the opportunity to do is to go in and edit some details about themselves that are then listed as coming from the verified source of that developer."
The feature stops short of letting developers add themselves back if they were dropped from a game's credits entirely after moving on.
Developers have long grappled with the industry practice of cutting them from game credits, even if they worked on that particular game for many years. For example, Donkey Kong Country Returns HD's credits were missing the original game's development staff and in 2023, former Retro Studios engineer Zoid Kirsch said he was "let down" by the lack of individual credits in Metroid Prime Remastered.
Meanwhile, translators contracted from firms outside of Nintendo voiced their disappointment at not being credited for work on high-profile games, too.
MobyGames' Professional tier costs $14.99 a month (or $11.99 a month with an annual subscription), but there's currently a 45-day free trial period.

item.title: A US District Judge has granted Nintendo a £3.4 million ($4.5m) default judgment against James Williams, the former Reddit moderator known online as "Archbox", after he failed to respond to a lawsuit over alleged Nintendo Switch piracy. Read more
item.description:
A US District Judge has granted Nintendo a £3.4 million ($4.5m) default judgment against James Williams, the former Reddit moderator known online as "Archbox", after he failed to respond to a lawsuit over alleged Nintendo Switch piracy.
After putting Switch pirate Gary Bowser behind bars and targeting emulator software Yuzu, back in 2024 Nintendo hunted down alleged Switch pirate James "Archbox" Williams, the main moderator behind r/SwitchPirates, by tracking his Reddit posts.
By this time last year, court papers revealed Nintendo was seeking $4.5m in damages from Williams, accusing him of having "facilitated a network of unauthorised 'shops'...that have offered to the public extensive libraries of pirated Nintendo Switch games for download".
And now, according to TorrentFreak, $4.5 million (£3.4m) is exactly what Williams now owes Nintendo.
The judge noted that while Williams had not responded to the lawsuit, he must have been aware of it given he had hired a lawyer to object to a Google subpoena.
Nintendo asked for $150,000 for every one of the 30 games Williams allegedly pirated, including The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, Mario Kart 8 Deluxe and Super Smash Bros. Ultimate, adding up to the full $4.5 million (£3.4m). The judge agreed, ruling that "Williams' egregious infringement activities merit substantial punishment here" and issued a permanent injunction barring Williams from distributing any pirated Nintendo games, not just the 30 named titles, and from encouraging anyone else to do so.
The judge also credited Nintendo for not separately seeking DMCA damages or attorneys' fees, calling it a "gesture of reasonableness" that supported awarding the maximum copyright damages.
Last month, John Romero, the co-founder of id Software and father of game series Quake and Doom, recounted a tale about when id Software worked with Taiwanese pirates to spread Doom.

item.title: Hello and welcome back to our regular feature where we write a little about the games we've been playing. item.description:
Hello and welcome back to our regular feature where we write a little about the games we've been playing. This week, Bertie's still pretending to be a vampire, Kelsey's been breeding an army of cats, Mat's been melting mounted warriors, Marie's been a willing accomplice, and Connor's been smitten all over again.
But enough of that: what have you been playing this week?
And don't forget we have an entire dusty archive of previous What We've Been Playings, just in case you don't trust your memory any more and want to check which games you've played and see what you thought of them.
I'm still playing Dawnwalker in any spare moment I get, which I think is an encouraging sign - that I still want to play a game after reviewing it. I loaded an old save so I could continue exploring the world and find new things. And I am finding new things - I've come across some brilliantly bizarre quests and encounters.
But the most bizarre moments have been unintended - from bugs. One quest broke during review and it locked two NPCs in never-ending combat, so the quest related to them was never completed. I tried everything to budge it but nothing worked. However, when I played the other day, it was fixed. The problem was, the game yanked me from another quest in order to resolve it, which nearly broke the other quest for me.
I had to painstakingly retrace my steps to find the route to the underground area I'd been in, then slightly exploit the game using a vampire blink ability to get behind a bookshelf now blocking my way. It took hours of work; I was strangely elated when I managed it. Now to fix a broken Sacred Stone ritual that's rendered a chunk of my world impassable because of a magical storm permanently raging there...
Mewgenics arrived on consoles a few weeks ago, and given that I play Edmund McMillen's The Binding of Isaac mostly handheld, I figured it a good idea to give Mewgenics a whirl handheld too.
I can confirm I have zero regrets. As soon as I realised Mewgenics supported the Switch 2's touch screen, any spare time that I did have has since gone out the window entirely while I curl up on my sofa and breed my army of battle cats. Between that and playing Silent Hill Townfall for work - which has been an absolute blast - I've been having a great time with games lately. At the cost of my social life, that is.
The best bits of Fire Emblem games are so good. Min-maxing your characters stats for extremely specific, but oddly common events. I've got a heavily defensive unit with a sword that melts through mounted units, so they take no damage on the enemy turn but wreck them all before even needing to move again. I've given one of my archers a ring that increases dodge-chance against units using bows themselves, imagining some kind of string-weaponry version of Enemy at the Gates every time I put him in their domain.
Everything else feels like padding. The social link stuff is lovely, just a little break in-between combat for a cute little chat, reminding you about the sort of humanity that all this conflict is in the necessity of protecting. It's just all the wandering around. Yes, you can fast-travel to points of interest, but not to every quest-dealer. It's the sort of thing I bounced off Marvel's Midnight Sons for, not wanting to plod in a castle that could just be a menu, and it's something that's clearly a consideration in Star Wars Zero Company, which contains as much of it as you feel up to.The variety of stuff on offer is lovely. I just wish my play-sessions had more of the stuff I’m actually there to do.
Sometimes you need to just sit down and help a goose on its mission to spread fear. Stealing toys off a table, locking a small child in a phone booth, honking at the gardener to get them out of your way while you move a welly-boot as a distraction before stealing something else. Come to think of it, this goose is a criminal genius and I'm definitely enjoying being a chaos-helping accomplice.
I have been captured by World of Warcraft yet again, despite my best efforts. What started as a brief exploration into what all the fuss was about has become a fixture of my evenings. Evenings meant for going outside are now spent killing boars and running dungeons.
It's only a brief window into the full game at this time, a level one-to-20 slice of the full journey, but it has made a strong first impression on me. I'm a big fan of the new Skyborne starting zone Zephras Isle as well. Its flowing grasslands and towering celestial pillars make for dramatic framing, especially with the new lighting effects.
I cannot wait until November when Forever fully comes out. I do believe it may eat my life entirely. But that's okay; nothing else is coming out in November anyway.

item.description:
Skyrim launched almost 15 years ago while The Elder Scrolls 6 is still marinating over at Bethesda Game Studios. Even so, Bethesda apparently never considered having an outside team develop a spin-off game to fill that painfully long gap - as it did once upon a time with Obsidian's Fallout: New Vegas.
That's according to Kurt Kuhlmann, a lead Skyrim developer and the fantasy series' former loremaster, who told the FRVR podcast that Bethesda is apparently too protective over its golden goose to let anyone else tackle a mainline-style game.
Kuhlmann said Fallout: New Vegas - often considered the best Fallout game in many circles - created lots of discussion around which company did it best. Bethesda or Obsidian? "There are the Obsidian, New Vegas people that think obviously New Vegas is way better, Obsidian is way better at making those games and, 'Why don't they just get Fallout altogether?'"
Bethesda supposedly didn't want those sentiments to follow The Elder Scrolls, as well - Kuhlmann said he doesn't think director Todd Howard "wanted to create that situation again."
"Todd, from my time there, he is very protective of it," Kuhlmann added. "I do think [The Elder Scrolls Online] took the heat off… there was a new Elder Scrolls product and it was ongoing. It was creating new content constantly. There are a lot of people, I mean, I know the single-player people, I'm one of those people–but there are a lot of people to whom The Elder Scrolls is now ESO. That’s their experience with it. That's what they love. That's where they got their Elder Scrolls gaming experience, and that's probably what they want more of."
It's worth noting that the former Elder Scrolls loremaster left the studio in 2023, and a lot has changed at Bethesda in the years since. Corporate owner Xbox is reportedly more focused on its biggest of big games nowadays, Fallout and The Elder Scrolls included. As part of the company's ongoing restructure and mass layoffs, Obsidian is now under the Bethesda umbrella and is even working on a new Fallout game. Perhaps there's room for a spin-off sometime after The Elder Scrolls 6 eventually comes out, though Bethesda president Jill Braff recently told staff Obsidian's "creative identity and strengths" will remain intact following the move.

item.description:
Resident Evil Requiem is still doing bonkers business while elongating Capcom's generational win streak, but the new big-screen reboot didn't make as big of an impact on game sales as you might expect. Still, according to estimates from Alinea Analytics, the ninth mainline game in the horror series has made over $500m (around £377m) and counting.
Alinea Analytics' Rhys Elliott today reported that Resident Evil Requiem has crossed the $500m mark, according to estimates from the industry analyst, which means it's outpacing every other Resident Evil game to date and is close to catching up to Leon Kennedy's last blockbuster. Resident Evil 4's remake has supposedly made more than $600m after three years, for comparison.
Some other interesting stats: Resident Evil Requiem's most popular platform is reportedly PS5. Not too surprising considering the series' tight corridors and even tighter camera angles began giving everyone the spooks on the very first PlayStation console. Requiem's sold 4m copies on PS5, 30% of which come from physical copies, despite Sony's disc-less future.
But what about the new Resident Evil film? Did it give Requiem a push? While Zach Cregger's new reboot set a series-best opening weekend, pulling in over $108m worldwide, it didn't move the needle too much as far as game sales go. Or, at least, it didn't move the needle as much as Capcom's very generous (and fairly frequent) discounts.
Funnily enough, Capcom began selling multiple Resident Evil games at a discounted price eight days before the film debuted on cinema screens. By the time the film's opening weekend rolled around, Requiem began making 4% less money per day on PS5. "From about $284k to $271k," according to the report, since the slightly increased demand didn't cancel out the game's lower-than-usual price.
Cregger's Resident Evil did give all games in the series a bump in daily players, however - and the older, non-Requiem ones also sold more during its opening. Resident Evil 2's remake was reportedly the biggest benefactor, as it enjoyed 48% more players than normal across all platforms once the film was in cinemas. The game's Raccoon City setting and the fact that it's generally a pretty great game helped, too. Resident Evil 3's remake, the one that doesn't slap quite so hard, saw a 25% jump in players.

Control Resonant's upside down world is out now, but Remedy Entertainment's not done with the RPG just yet. The Alan Wake and Max Payne maker has detailed some of its post-launch plans for the game, which currently include new outfits, a Photo Mode and a New Game Plus Plus option for anyone who wants to carry their progress over into neverending playthroughs.
Control Resonant's current New Game Plus mode lets you keep most of Dylan Faden's paranatural upgrades in a fresh playthrough - except for traversal abilities, which would likely lead to messy sequence breaks. "We're preparing an update that will add... wait for it... New Game++, which means you can start NG+ run after NG+ run, without needing to erase all your progress," Remedy wrote. "Do 665 runs if you want!"
An update in November should also bring a much-needed Photo Mode to the game. Remedy's worlds are always gorgeous and Control Resonant's freaky, lopsided Manhattan is no different, so it's not surprising to hear players have been asking for a way to snap in-game pictures.
"We hear you, you want it, and we want to get it into your hands," said Remedy. The studio's apparently been cooking the feature for a while and have even consulted real-life virtual photographers, but Photo Mode didn't make the cut on day one "because we needed to prioritize making sure the game was in the best possible shape."
Finally, Remedy is also working on more cosmetics for Dylan. "We've seen some... eclectic outfit combinations. You can look forward to more cosmetic pieces for our favorite former coma patient/prisoner/fashion icon in future updates," Remedy said, though it didn't put out a release window for those of you treating Resonant like a dress-up sim.
Be sure to check out our full Control Resonant walkthrough if you're currently zipping across the game's twisty-turvy buildings.
Eurogamer's Control Resonant review said it's "a more action-RPG oriented follow-up to Control, but in leaving the Oldest House it also leaves behind some of what gave the original its magic."

item.description:
Ubisoft Milan, the studio behind the acclaimed Mario + Rabbids games, reportedly came close to making a Zelda spin-off starring the series' biggest villain, Ganondorf, instead of regular protagonist Link - but an initially receptive Nintendo eventually pulled the plug on the whole thing.
That's according to a new report from Insider Gaming, which claims Ubisoft Milan began working on the pitch in 2022, shortly after the launch of Mario + Rabbids Sparks of Hope. Despite the Mario-themed turn-based strategy sequel's modest sales, it's said Nintendo and Ubisoft Milan began discussing another potential collaboration soon after.
According to "sources familiar with the discussions", Mario + Rabbids co-creator Davide Soliani had considerably greater ambitions this time around, and Ubisoft Milan spent the winter developing "what they deemed the perfect pitch" for Project Goliath - a new The Legend of Zelda spin-off that was to star a brand-new character as its protagonist.
Supposedly, Nintendo liked the concept but asked the team to replace their own character with Link's archnemesis, Ganondorf. Work continued, but in November 2023, Nintendo reportedly rejected Ubisoft Milan's prototype, turning the project into a what-could-have-been. As to why Nintendo ultimately said no, the reasons behind the decision "remain unclear".
After that, another project based on a Nintendo IP was supposedly discussed - rumours ranged from a new Star Fox game to another Mario spin-off - but "between late 2023 and early 2024, conversations between Nintendo and Ubisoft began to break down." With the project dead, members of the team were reportedly dispersed across the wider company to work on other things, and Davide Soliani - a 25-year Ubisoft veteran at that point - made the decision to leave the publisher and establish his own studio, Day 4 Night.
Since then, Ubisoft Milan has been collaborating with Ubisoft Montpellier on the promising Rayman Legends Untold. As for Ganondorf, his dreams of starring in his own Zelda spin-off have yet to be fulfilled, but perhaps it's an idea Nintendo might choose to revisit in some other place and time.

item.description:
Embark Studios has announced a new matchmaking test for Arc Raiders that'll allow players to opt into a PvE version featuring none of the usual player-versus-player violence. It's the developer's response to a growing portion of the playerbase apparently uninterested in hurting their raiders-in-arms.
In a blog post on the official Arc Raiders website, executive producer Aleksander Grøndal revealed the studio's PvE test will run from 13th to 20th October, and will enable participants to choose between the new, friendlier version of Arc Raiders and the regular, more ruthless version.
Grøndal goes on to recap Arc Raiders' origin as a raid-based co-op PvE shooter with looting mechanics, and Embark's eventual decision to shift towards the extraction shooter we know today. However, in an interesting twist of fate, it turns out many players are approaching the game with a collaborative mindset despite the incentives to kill their fellow players, turning it into what Grøndal calls the "Extraction (Don’t) Shooter".
He further breaks down this phenomenon with statistics, highlighting that around 37 percent of raiders are friendly co-op players, and that this figure has grown since launch. In comparison, around 34 percent are PvP-focused - a figure that has stayed consistent since launch - and the remaining 27 or so percent of raiders are a mix between the two. So there's clearly demand for more formalised PvE.
Enter Embark's new test, and a PvE mode that'll allow for solo, duos, and trios to queue it out. Some map conditions, like night raids and hidden bunkers, will be absent as they were designed with PvP in mind. Additionally, loot value in PvE matchmaking will be lessened to take into account the reduced danger players face by playing this way.
On this front, Grøndal acknowledges some risks with this test, saying the studio will - given the amount of relatively risk-free loot players can potentially extract with - be keeping a close eye on the wider player economy. It'll be watching matchmaking times during the test too.
Finally, Grøndal notes the test does not mean a permanent PvE mode will be added in the future. Instead, he describes it as "indication that we are seriously considering it."
It's an interesting move by Arc Raiders. The game was extremely popular at launch, and continued to retain a strong playerbase in the months following. Almost immediately, the game gained notoriety due to its strangely friendly community, a distinct difference from other extraction shooters.
Some will look at this shift - which coincides with Marathon's recent announcement of a PvE mode - as an indicator of wider trends away from the hardcore PvP extraction genre. However there's a clear difference here. While Arc Raiders is certainly not as popular as it once was, this reads more like a reactive accommodation to the game's community, rather than a necessary push to win back lost players.
If Embark does decide to embrace PvE as a permanent game mode, one does wonder how it would impact future updates, and how it might create updates with both PvP and PvE players in mind. Would matchmaking become more fierce as a result? An interesting question for the future.

item.description:
Sound the alarm! Alert your loved ones! Nearly 18 years after its original announcement, Beyond Good & Evil 2 apparently still isn't dead, according to a Ubisoft Bordeaux developer who says he's been working on the game for months.
Beyond Good & Evil 2 was originally unveiled back in 2008, and has seemingly been stuck in development hell ever since. However, last year brought new signs of life when a fresh job posting for the game appeared online. And now, after another lengthy lull in updates, lead writer and associate narrative director Rik Godwin has confirmed (as spotted by IGN) the project is still in development. With Ubisoft's permission, of course.
"Odd sort of non-announcement but for the past few months I've been working on Beyond Good & Evil 2 in a support/consultant role, Godwin wrote on social media. "I am allowed to say this, I checked."
The current state of Beyond Good & Evil 2 remains a mystery, and the overall question of whether it's dead or not has confounded onlookers for years.
Since its unveiling in 2008, we've had a flashy E3 cinematic trailer, which was shared the following year. Later, Joseph Gordon Levitt's Hit Record announced a - briefly controversial - partnership with Ubisoft which would allow artists to submit works for use in the game. In 2022, the game overtook Duke Nukem Forever in the Guiness Book of Records as the longest game in-development. There was a further flurry of news in January 2023 when Ubisoft insisted Beyond Good & Evil 2 still existed, and gameplay footage emerged that September via an animator's portfolio.
Since then, Ubisoft has continued to sporadically insist, with little evidence, Beyond Good & Evil 2 remains in development, with its latest reassurance (save for Godwin's post) coming in January of this year.
Perhaps we may still yet see Beyond Good & Evil 2 emerge from this mire. There's a strange nostalgia writing about its ongoing development; I remember seeing its cinematic E3 trailer back in 2018 - I was 20-years-old at the time! Now I'm nearing 30 with a beard. Hopefully Jade has fared better. One can hope!
